How I built a reliable solution that reads real OTP emails using IMAP while keeping the full login flow intact.
Press enter or click to view image in full size

Secure real email verification without mocks or manual steps.Every login flow protected by email-based OTP eventually creates the same problem for test automation: a human has to open an inbox, read a code, and type it in within a few minutes. That doesn’t scale, and it definitely doesn’t run in CI on a schedule.
For our end-to-end suite, I built a solution that goes through the real login path — no mocked auth, no bypass flag — by giving Playwright direct, secure access to the test mailbox itself.
The Stack

• @playwright/test — drives the browser: enters credentials, submits the form, types the OTP, waits for navigation, asserts success.

• imapflow — connects securely to the mailbox over IMAP and searches for the verification email.

• mailparser — parses the raw MIME message into readable text.

• dotenv — loads mailbox and application credentials from a git-ignored .env file, so nothing sensitive touches source control.

• A regular expression to pull the OTP digits out of the parsed email body.
The application’s OTP screen is built with Chakra UI’s PinInput component, which is why the test types the full code with a short delay between keystrokes rather than filling each digit box independently — that’s what lets the component’s internal state and focus management behave the way it would for a real user.
How it works
A shared login() helper drives the flow:

• Playwright opens the app and locates the login fields via data-testid selectors.

• It submits email and password.

• It waits for either the OTP screen to appear, or a direct redirect past it — because some test accounts have OTP disabled entirely, and should skip mailbox access altogether.
When OTP is required, a separate fetchLoginOtp() helper takes over:

• Opens a secure IMAP connection to the mailbox and locks the inbox while inspecting it.

• Filters to messages from the app’s known sender address.

• Checks the five most recent matches.

• Accepts only messages with the expected “Login Verification” subject.

• Rejects anything sent before the current login attempt — this is what prevents the test from accidentally reusing a stale code from a previous run.

• Parses the email with mailparser and extracts the code with:
JavaScript
/OTP code is:\s*(\d{4})/iThe mailbox is polled every two seconds until a configured timeout. Once the code arrives, Playwright types it into the PinInput, submits, and confirms success by waiting for the post-login URL.
Reliability details that actually matter
The parts that make this safe to run unattended in CI aren’t the happy path — they’re the edge cases:

• Stale-email filtering — only messages created after the login request count.

• Mailbox locking — the inbox is locked for the duration of the search/fetch.

• Guaranteed cleanup — the IMAP connection closes in a finally block even on failure.

• Expiration handling — polling races against the OTP screen timing out.

• Automatic retry — expired, delayed, or rejected codes trigger a fresh login attempt, up to three tries.

• Mixed-account support — accounts with OTP disabled are detected and skipped automatically.

• Environment-aware selectors — local and deployed login pages can differ without breaking the test.
One real constraint worth knowing
Tests can’t request OTP codes concurrently for the same account. Two parallel runs hitting one mailbox can race for the same email and end up selecting — or invalidating — each other’s code. In practice, this means OTP-enabled test accounts need to be dedicated to a single active test run at a time, which shapes how you allocate accounts across a parallel test suite.
What’s your approach?
A fixed test-only OTP, a local mail catcher like Mailpit, or going straight to a real mailbox like this? Trade-offs on all three are real, and I’d like to hear what’s worked for others.
